blocks.text: Writing a good prompt template is only half the job. The other half is registering it with the SDK so the server actually knows the prompt exists, can describe it to a client, and can run its handler when asked.

Registration is the small ceremony that turns a plain function into something a client can discover and call over MCP. Get the shape right once, and adding a second or third related prompt becomes almost mechanical.

This lesson walks through exactly what a registration call needs, how a handler builds a list of messages instead of a single string, and how to confirm everything works through prompts/list and prompts/get.
1. What Registering a Prompt Actually Means

blocks.alt: What Registering a Prompt Actually Means
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012146-997267744.png
Registering a prompt means telling the server, at startup, that this particular name exists, what it does, what arguments it takes, and which function should run when a client asks for it.
Once registered, the server keeps that prompt in an internal list it can show to any client that asks, and can look up instantly the moment a prompts/get request names it.
Nothing about registration touches a model directly. It only wires a name to a function, the actual conversation with a model happens later, once a client sends the returned messages onward.
2. The Four Ingredients a Registration Call Needs

blocks.alt: The Four Ingredients a Registration Call Needs
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012147-391298023.png
Every SDK, whichever language it is written in, asks for the same four things when you register a prompt: a name, a description, an arguments list, and a handler function.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Ingredient","What it is for"],"rows":[["Name","The stable identifier a client uses in prompts/get"],["Description","Plain text a client can show a person deciding whether to use this prompt"],["Arguments","The named inputs the handler expects, each with its own description"],["Handler","The function that turns those arguments into the final message list"]]}

blocks.text: Miss one of these and the SDK either refuses to register the prompt or produces a prompt a client cannot use sensibly.
3. Choosing a Clear, Stable Prompt Name
A prompt name is an identifier, not a sentence, so short lowercase words joined by underscores work best, for example draft_reply or summarize_ticket.
Once a name ships to real clients, treat it as a stable contract. Renaming it later breaks anyone who saved a call to the old name.
Two prompts with names that only differ by a letter or two are easy to mix up when scanning a long prompts/list result, so pick names that read clearly apart at a glance.
4. Writing a Description a Client Can Show Directly
The description is what a client renders in a prompt picker for a human, so it should say plainly what the prompt produces and when someone would reach for it.
A description like "Drafts a support reply for a ticket, in a chosen tone" tells a person everything they need. A description like "Reply prompt" tells them almost nothing.
5. Declaring the Arguments a Handler Will Receive
Each argument gets a name, a short description, and whether it is required. Every argument arrives as plain text, since that is what a prompt argument is built to hold.

items: name: the key the handler will look up in the arguments object
description: what value the client should collect from the user
required: whether the handler can run without it

blocks.text: The full rules around validating and defaulting these values get their own dedicated lesson. Here we only need enough to write a working handler.
6. The Handler Function: Turning Arguments into Messages

blocks.alt: The Handler Function: Turning Arguments into Messages
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012147-532161722.png
The handler is a plain function. It receives the arguments a client sent, does whatever lookup or formatting it needs, and returns the messages the client should send on to a model.
Nothing about the handler is special or magical. It is ordinary code, wired in through the registration call so the server knows to run it for that one prompt name.

A handler can call a database, read a file, or reach out to another service before building its messages. The SDK does not care what happens inside, only that the final return value is shaped correctly.
7. Handling Lookup Failures Inside a Handler
A handler often needs to look something up, a ticket, a note, a record, before it can build a sensible message. That lookup can fail even when every argument was valid.
Raising a clear error from inside the handler is the right move when a lookup fails, rather than quietly returning an empty or misleading message.
The SDK turns that raised error into a proper JSON-RPC error response, so the client sees exactly why prompts/get failed instead of an unhelpful blank result.
8. Registering a Prompt in Python with FastMCP
The Python SDK uses a decorator. Decorate a plain function with @mcp.prompt and its name, description and argument types are picked up automatically.
The function name becomes the prompt name, the docstring becomes the description, and the type hints describe the arguments, no separate schema needed.
9. Registering a Prompt in JavaScript or TypeScript
The TypeScript SDK takes the name, an argument schema built with Zod, and an async handler, all passed directly to server.prompt.

blocks.text: 10. Returning a Single Message vs Returning Several

blocks.alt: Returning a Single Message vs Returning Several
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012147-283072071.png
A handler is not limited to one message. It can return just a user message for something simple, or several messages when the prompt needs to set up context first.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Return shape","When it fits"],"rows":[["One user message","A short, self contained instruction with nothing extra to set up"],["System message plus user message","The prompt needs to set a persona or ground rules separately from the actual request"],["Several user and assistant turns","Seeding a short example conversation before the real question"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Building a System Message Plus a User Message

blocks.alt: Building a System Message Plus a User Message
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012814-944108033.png
A common and useful pattern is returning exactly two messages: a system message that sets tone and rules, followed by a user message carrying the actual request.
Splitting the two keeps the persona instructions separate from the specific task, which makes both easier to read and easier to change independently.

blocks.title: Order is part of the meaning
blocks.content: The array order is the conversation order. Put the system style message first so it frames the request before the user content arrives.

blocks.text: 12. The Shape of Each Message: Role and Content
Every message a handler returns has exactly two parts: a role, usually system, user or assistant, and content, the actual text.
Some SDKs let a handler return plain strings for convenience and wrap them into this shape automatically, but the shape underneath is always role plus content.
13. Registering Several Related Prompts Without Repeating Yourself

blocks.alt: Registering Several Related Prompts Without Repeating Yourself
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012814-284601681.png
Once a second and third prompt show up for the same domain, small shared helpers keep the code from turning into repeated dict literals everywhere.

items: Give each prompt its own small handler function rather than one giant function branching on a name
Share tiny helpers like sys_msg and usr_msg instead of repeating the same dict shape everywhere
Keep each prompt focused on one job so a client can pick between them by description alone

blocks.text: 14. What prompts/list Shows the Client
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012815-76966127.png
Every registered prompt shows up automatically in the result of prompts/list, with its name, description and full arguments array, no extra work required.
15. Confirming prompts/get Returns What You Expect
Calling prompts/get with a name and arguments should hand back exactly the messages the handler built, in order, ready to send to a model.
16. Writing a Small Manual Test Before Shipping
Before calling a new prompt done, connect a test client, call prompts/list and confirm the new name and description appear correctly.
Then call prompts/get with a valid set of arguments and read the returned messages exactly as a model would receive them, checking role order and wording.

code.content:
# Manual checklist for a newly registered prompt
# 1. Call prompts/list, confirm name, description and arguments look right
# 2. Call prompts/get with valid arguments, confirm messages come back in the expected order
# 3. Confirm the system message, if any, always appears before the user message
# 4. Repeat prompts/get with a second, different set of arguments to check the template actually changes

blocks.text: 17. Where Registration Code Should Live
For a server with only one or two prompts, registering them right next to the tools in a single file is perfectly fine.
Once a server grows past a handful of prompts, moving them into their own module, one file per domain, keeps the main server file readable and makes it obvious where to add the next one.
However you organize the files, importing all the prompt modules once at startup, before the server starts accepting connections, keeps registration simple and predictable.
Worked Example
Picture a small notes server that wants one prompt, summarize_note, taking a single required argument, note_id.

After registering it, prompts/list should show summarize_note with its description and the single note_id argument. Calling prompts/get with a real note_id should return exactly two messages, system then user, ready to hand to a model.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to return the messages in the shape the SDK expects, for example a bare string where an array of role and content objects is required
Putting the user message before the system message, which changes how a model reads the framing
Giving two different prompts nearly identical names that are easy to confuse when scanning prompts/list
Writing a description that just repeats the prompt name instead of explaining what it produces
Copying the same message building code into every handler instead of sharing one small helper
Never actually calling prompts/get during testing and only reading the handler code by eye

blocks.text: Practice
Register a new prompt named explain_error that takes a required error_message argument and an optional audience argument, defaulting to a general reader.

Have its handler return a system message describing the tone to use for that audience, followed by a user message asking for a plain language explanation of the error. Then write out what prompts/get should return for a call with only error_message supplied.
Finally, sketch what prompts/list should show for explain_error, and check that its description alone would be enough for someone to guess when to use it.
Key Takeaway

Registering a prompt is just wiring a name, description, arguments and handler into the server, so the handler can turn a request into an ordered list of messages, often a system message followed by a user message.
A prompt is not really finished until you have watched it appear correctly in prompts/list and checked its messages coming back from prompts/get.
